opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it as a cost-benefit question.

The case for logits is that they carry far more information per token than a sampled sequence. With hard labels from teacher samples, the student only learns "this token was chosen." With the full distribution, it learns how plausible the alternatives were: which near-synonyms are fine, where the teacher is uncertain, where it's confident. That "dark knowledge," in Hinton's phrase, makes distillation much more sample-efficient, especially for smaller students that can't absorb everything from limited data.

But there are a few things I check before deciding it's worth it.

**First, do you actually have access, and can you afford it?** Storing full-vocabulary logits for every token is enormous at a 100k+ vocabulary. In practice people keep the top-k, maybe 20 to 100 tokens, or compute teacher logits on the fly. If you're distilling from a closed API model, you often only get text or a few log-probs, so the question answers itself.

**Second, how compatible are the teacher and student?** If they share a tokenizer, token-level KL is straightforward. If they don't, you need some alignment scheme, and a lot of the benefit can disappear in the mismatch. Sequence-level distillation on teacher outputs becomes much more attractive then.

**Third, how big is the capacity gap?** If the student is much weaker, forcing it to match the teacher's full distribution with forward KL can make it spread probability over things it can't model well, and you get blurry, hallucination-prone generations. That's where the divergence choice matters: reverse KL or something like generalized JSD lets the student be more mode-seeking and focus on what it can represent.

**Fourth, and the one I care about most: whose distribution are you training on?** Classic distillation computes teacher logits on fixed teacher-generated or ground-truth sequences. At inference, though, the student generates its own prefixes and makes mistakes the teacher never would. That train-inference mismatch is exposure bias. On-policy distillation fixes it: sample from the student, then have the teacher score those student tokens with its logits. You get dense, per-token feedback on exactly the states the student will visit. In my experience that's where teacher logits pay off most, because the teacher is effectively a dense reward model correcting the student's own errors.

So my rule of thumb: if you share a tokenizer, can afford teacher forward passes, and the student will generate long sequences where errors compound, logits, especially on-policy, are almost always worth it. If you only have black-box text access or a huge tokenizer mismatch, start with fine-tuning on good teacher samples, then add RL or preference signals on top.

The last thing I'd say is to measure it empirically. Run a small ablation: same compute, hard-label SFT versus logit distillation versus on-policy distillation, evaluated on the generation tasks you care about, not just held-out perplexity. Perplexity can look great with forward KL while sampled outputs get worse, so the eval needs to match how the model will actually be used.

r001.rationale: It explicitly treats the student’s capacity gap as a deciding factor and explains how a much weaker student may struggle to match the teacher’s full distribution.

r002.rationale: It describes on-policy distillation as addressing train–inference mismatch and says teacher logits pay off most there; it also names divergence choices that can improve how logits are used.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that it depends on what you're trying to get out of the distillation, and I think people often reach for logits by default without asking that question.

The classic argument for logits is the "dark knowledge" one from Hinton's original work: the full distribution over tokens tells you not just what the teacher picked, but what it considered plausible, and that's a much richer training signal than a single hard target. For language models that argument is real, but it comes with practical caveats. The vocabularies have to match, or you need some alignment trick. You need access to the teacher's forward pass, which rules out API-only teachers. And the storage and compute cost of materializing full distributions over a fifty- or hundred-thousand-token vocabulary is nontrivial, so people end up doing top-k truncation, which throws away part of what you wanted in the first place.

The bigger issue I'd point to is the distribution mismatch problem. If you do standard distillation on a fixed dataset of teacher outputs, the student is learning to match the teacher on the teacher's own trajectories. But at inference time the student is generating its own sequences, and once it makes a mistake it's in a region the teacher never showed it how to handle. This is the exposure bias story, and it's where on-policy distillation comes in. You sample from the student, and then you use the teacher's feedback on those student-generated sequences. That's where logits become genuinely valuable, because you get a dense, per-token signal on exactly the states the student actually visits. Compared to just doing sequence-level distillation with reinforcement-learning-style reward, the token-level distribution gives you a lot more gradient information per sample.

So my rough heuristic is this. If you're in a setting where the teacher and student share a tokenizer, you control the teacher, and you can afford to run it online, then logits are worth it, especially combined with sampling from the student. If you're in an API-restricted setting or the vocabularies differ, sequence-level distillation on teacher samples is often surprisingly competitive, and you shouldn't feel bad about using it. Sometimes with a strong teacher and enough data, the gap between the two is smaller than people expect, and the thing that matters more is whether you're training on student-generated data at all.

The other thing I'd flag is the choice of divergence. Forward KL, which is what you get with standard logit matching, is mode-covering. The student tries to spread probability mass everywhere the teacher does, and if the student is much smaller it can't, so it ends up with a smeared-out distribution that produces worse samples. Reverse KL or something like a generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence is mode-seeking, and for a capacity-constrained student that's often what you actually want. So "are logits worth it" is partially "which objective on those logits," and that second question is underrated.

r001.rationale: The response says a much smaller student may produce a smeared distribution under forward KL and notes that reverse KL may suit a capacity-constrained student, identifying student capacity as relevant to the choice and usefulness of logits.

r002.rationale: It presents on-policy distillation—using teacher feedback on student-generated sequences—as a setting where logits become especially valuable, and describes the denser token-level signal they provide.

astra-6.text:
I’d treat it as an empirical question: how much additional signal do the teacher’s logits give you over simply training on its generated answers? The attraction is that logits tell you more than which token the teacher chose. They also tell you which alternatives it considered plausible. But extracting, storing, and training on those distributions has a cost.

So I’d start with a strong baseline using teacher-generated responses, then compare that with logit-based distillation under a comparable compute budget. I’d look at the tasks we actually care about, not just how closely the student matches the teacher’s distribution. The teacher–student capacity gap and the data distribution matter, too; a small student may not be able to use all that extra information.

If logits consistently improve downstream performance enough to justify the overhead, I’d use them. If generating more or better training examples gets you a larger gain for the same budget, I’d prioritize that.

r001.rationale: It says the teacher–student capacity gap matters and that a small student may not be able to use all the extra information in logits.

r002.rationale: It weighs logits against generated answers and training examples, but does not say that improved distillation methods could make logits substantially more useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what the logits give you beyond the teacher’s sampled answer. They tell you which alternatives the teacher considers plausible, and that can provide a richer training signal. But that signal has to justify the cost of computing, storing, and transferring it, especially with a large vocabulary.

So I’d compare against a strong baseline that trains on teacher-generated responses, under the same overall budget. Then I’d check whether using logits improves the student on the tasks we actually care about. One important variable is where those logits are evaluated: on teacher-generated sequences, or on sequences the student generates itself. On the student’s own sequences, the teacher can provide feedback on situations the student actually encounters.

Ultimately, I wouldn’t assume logits are worth using just because they contain more information. I’d want to see that information translate into better student performance per unit of cost.

r001.rationale: The response discusses student performance and the sequences used for distillation, but does not identify student-model capacity as a factor in whether logits are useful.

r002.rationale: It recommends evaluating logits empirically, but does not suggest that improved distillation methods could make them substantially more useful.
